cashProfit.title: Cash profit vs statutory net income
cashProfit.content:
Cash profit is ANZ's own non-IFRS measure of underlying performance -- statutory net profit adjusted to remove items management judges non-representative of ongoing operations (hedge accounting timing, economic hedges of revenue/expense in foreign currency, and other one-off gains or losses).

For ANZ Group Holdings Limited: cash profit is the number analysts model, dividends are framed against, and management guidance targets -- not statutory NPAT. FY2025 cash profit fell to $5,787m against a statutory NetIncome of $5,891m, a narrower gap than in some prior years but still the one to reconcile before comparing to guidance.

What to watch:

  • A widening gap between cash profit and statutory net income (larger or more frequent add-backs)
  • Cash profit growth versus revenue growth -- is the gap coming from cost discipline or from below-the-line adjustments

creditImpairment.title: Credit impairment charge / (release)
creditImpairment.content:
The credit impairment charge is the bank's provisioning expense for expected loan losses in the period -- a positive number is a charge against profit; a negative number is a release of previously held provisions.

For ANZ Group Holdings Limited: this line is the credit cycle in one series. It spiked to $2,738m in FY2020 (COVID provisioning), then ran negative through FY2021-22 as those provisions were released back through profit, and has been rebuilding gradually since (FY2025: $441m). A rising charge with a growing loan book (see Customer Deposits vs Net Loans) is normal seasoning; a rising charge against a flat book signals asset-quality deterioration.

What to watch:

  • The charge as a proportion of the loan book (basis points), not just the absolute figure
  • Direction relative to unemployment and housing-market conditions in ANZ's core Australia/NZ markets

depositsLoans.title: Customer deposits vs net loans and advances
depositsLoans.content:
Customer deposits are the funding side of the balance sheet; net loans and advances are the asset side -- the loan book those deposits (plus wholesale funding) support.

For ANZ Group Holdings Limited: both have grown steadily -- deposits from $588bn (FY2016) to $955bn and net loans from $576bn to $829bn (FY2025) -- with deposits consistently exceeding loans, i.e. a loan-to-deposit ratio below 100% and no structural reliance on wholesale markets to fund lending growth. The FY2024 jump in loans reflects the Suncorp Bank acquisition completing.

What to watch:

  • Loan growth materially outpacing deposit growth (funding gap widening)
  • Loan book composition shifts (mortgage vs institutional/commercial) disclosed in the filings, not visible in this aggregate

costToIncome.title: Operating expenses vs revenue
costToIncome.content:
Operating expenses against revenue -- the numerator and denominator of the cost-to-income ratio banks are judged on.

For ANZ Group Holdings Limited: expenses jumped from $10,669m (FY2024) to $13,023m (FY2025) on Suncorp Bank integration costs and continued technology/remediation spend, outpacing revenue growth over the same period and compressing OperatingMargin from 46.0% to 39.3% -- the margin chart above shows the effect, this chart shows the two lines driving it.

What to watch:

  • Whether the FY2025 step-up in costs is integration-related and normalises, or is a new run-rate
  • Cost growth versus revenue growth each period (the cost-to-income ratio's direction)

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For ANZ Group Holdings Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For ANZ Group Holdings Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For ANZ Group Holdings Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For ANZ Group Holdings Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For ANZ Group Holdings Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For ANZ Group Holdings Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For ANZ Group Holdings Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For ANZ Group Holdings Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For ANZ Group Holdings Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
